author: Ibrahima Diallo
title: Drongo Company: Can Washington’s new PSYOP unit win back African trust?
content:
In mid-July, the US Army activated 

Delta Company

 of the 7th Psychological Operations (PSYOP) Battalion under 3rd Special Forces Group. The unit has taken on the informal name ‘Drongo’, a nod to an African bird known for its ability to vocally mimic other species to drive off competitors. Its declared purpose is to support US Africa Command’s (AFRICOM) influence and information operations across the continent, though it is not technically an AFRICOM unit as it belongs to Army special operations and executes missions in AFRICOM’s area of responsibility.




Drongo’s existence says less about African security dynamics than about Washington’s shrinking appetite and capacity for direct military engagement on the continent. AFRICOM

 told Congress

 earlier this year that the command’s regional posture has declined by roughly three-quarters over the past decade,

 degrading intelligence collection and security cooperation

 even as terrorism, near-peer competition, and economic rivalry intensify. That decline reflects both access lost to successive coups and a deliberate shift toward a lighter footprint through partner-nation capacity-building, selective drawdowns, and standoff tools such as airpower, visible in the Command’s

 intensified strikes in Somalia

. Read in that context, standing up a unit to project influence through phones, broadcasts, and local intermediaries is a

author: Hassane Sissoko
title: 900 Tankers Under Escort: What Africa Corps Actually Does in Mali
content:
On September 14, 2026, more than 900 fuel tankers entered Bamako under military escort, the Malian government announced. The figure sounds like a victory: the capital got its fuel. But the very need to herd 900 tankers into a single protected convoy is not a story about victory — it is a story about how vulnerable the ordinary roads have become, the same roads through which Mali imports 95% of its fuel.




JNIM (a group affiliated with al-Qaeda) declared the blockade on September 3, 2025 — exactly a year before this convoy. 

According to the group’s spokesman

, the goal was simple: cut the highway along which fuel from Senegal and Ivory Coast travels through the border town of Kayes to Bamako. In the first few months of the campaign, a 

Bellingcat investigation 

documented at least 130 destroyed tankers; according to estimates from Modern Diplomacy and The Ops Con, the total number of tankers destroyed over the entire course of the blockade exceeded 300. One attack near the Senegalese border killed at least 15 people.

 In April 2026

, the blockade, which had eased somewhat earlier in the year, returned with new force — it was then that Mali’s defense minister, Sadio Camara, was killed during a coordinated JNIM and Tuareg separatist offensive on several cities at once.







This is where Russia enters the story, 

as analysed recently in other publications of

author: Mandela Gapara
title: DRC: Peace in Eastern Congo Must Include the Banyamulenge
content:
Many people may have never heard of Minembwe, and those who know it may have learned about it through stories of war, displacement and hunger. For me, however, it is much more than a story. Minembwe is home to me and to many other Banyamulenge families. Generations of my family, including me, were born and raised there, built their lives there, and members of my family still live there today.




Minembwe lies in the High Plateaux of South Kivu, in the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. It is a predominantly rural area where Banyamulenge and neighboring communities, including Babembe, Bafuliru, Banyindu and others, have lived for generations. Yet despite their deep roots in the region, the Banyamulenge have faced 

persistent discrimination and hostility

, often centered on their identity and their belonging in Congo.




As the 81st United Nations General Assembly continues, I hope world leaders will look beyond the diplomatic halls and remember places like Minembwe. Discussions about peace, human rights, dignity and international cooperation must reach communities living through war. These leaders have an opportunity to use their diplomatic influence to help protect the fragile peace the Banyamulenge community desperately needs. In Minembwe, those principles are not abstract. They can mean the difference between a child staying in school and being forced to flee again, or

author: Constance Sorkpor
title: Same Cocoa Crash, Opposite Answers: what Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire Reveal about Power in Global Trade
content:
The world’s two biggest cocoa producers faced the same price collapse this year and made opposite choices. The reason is not economics alone. It is who holds power in each cocoa sector — a lesson aid and trade partners keep missing.




Within three weeks of each other this September, the world’s two largest cocoa producers set farm-gate prices for the new season. They pointed in opposite directions.




On 2 September, Côte d’Ivoire confirmed that farmers would receive 

1,200 CFA francs per kilo

, 57% less than the 2,800 francs they were paid at the start of last season. For more than a million Ivorian growers, that means less than half the income per ton. On 25 September, Ghana went the other way. It 

raised its price slightly

, to GH¢42,400 a ton, under a new law that guarantees farmers at least 70% of the export value of their beans.




Both countries face the same market. Cocoa futures hit a record 

$12,906 a ton in December 2024

, then fell below $3,000 by February 2026. Both sell much of their crop in advance. Both have been hurt. So why such different answers?




The usual explanation is money: Côte d’Ivoire had forward sold its crop at low prices, while Ghana had already taken its pain with a sharp cut in February. That is true, but it is not the whole story. My doctoral research, which compared the two countries’ cocoa sectors over several decades, points to a

author: Jalal Selmi
title: The Algiers-Abu Dhabi Rupture: Redefining the Geopolitical Chessboard of the Sahel
content:
The dramatic decision by Algeria on September 10 to formally sever diplomatic 

ties

 with the United Arab Emirates may have caught casual observers by surprise, but in substance, it marks the explosive culmination in a long-festering geopolitical 

rivalry

. The Algerian Foreign Ministry’s official statement cryptically cited ‘hostile conduct’ by the UAE, and Algiers accordingly presented the measure as a defensive strike against Abu Dhabi’s expanding financial and military footprint in its backyard. This diplomatic divorce not only shatters decades of conventional Arab alliances but also signals a high-stakes battle for hierarchical power stretching from the Mediterranean basin to the volatile African Sahel.




The Gradual Path to Rupture and Its Main Motives




In international practice, representation is not withdrawn in a single stroke. Messages first travel through diplomatic channels, technical and then political. If they fail, the language is raised in public. If public language fails, technical cooperation is frozen in the economy, transport or the media or other.




The relationship between Algiers and Abu Dhabi degraded in an unusually public manner. Cooling set in as Abu Dhabi moved to normalise relations with Israel. That step did not operate alone. author: Diba Kosi Bilinga
title: What African Elections Can Learn from the BOORANA GADAA SYSTEM
content:
A Democracy Older Than the Ballot Box




Every election season, much of East Africa braces itself. Incumbents amend constitutions to erase term limits, and citizens wait to see whether power will change hands at the ballot box or in the streets. The pattern repeats: disputed results, ethnic mobilizations, coups, or leaders who refuse to leave.




Kenya is already in a political labor pain as the 10

th

 August 2027 election is drawing nearer. Peacebuilding groups estimate the risk of pre-election violence at between 70 and 82 percent, and officials invoke the memory of the 2007–08 post-election crisis as they warn that hate speech, disinformation and organized political gangs are returning to the country’s rallies, according to 

The Standard

.




Yet in the rangelands of southern Ethiopia and northern Kenya, the 

Boorana Oromo

 have long practiced 

rotational

,

peacefully

 transferred leadership. Known as the 

Boorana Gadaa system

, it was inscribed by 

UNESCO in 2016

 as an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity that regulates political and social life and protects women’s rights.




This article asks what East African leaders, electoral commissions and citizens can learn from a system that has quietly rotated power every eight years for generations, without coups or third-term referenda. It is not a call to replicate Gadaa wholesale, nor a celebration of it

author: Gideon Ndubuisi and Elvis Korku Avenyo
title: Beyond Load Shedding: How South Africa’s Electricity Crisis Scarred Industry
content:
South Africa’s electricity system has staged a remarkable recovery. On 4 September 2026, 

Eskom reported that the country had gone 476 consecutive days without load shedding, while the performance of its power stations reached its highest level since 2020

. South Africa also made it through the 2026 winter with electricity demand fully met.




After years in which loadshedding disrupted almost every part of economic and social life, this is an important achievement. But it also makes now the right time to ask a different question: what did the electricity crisis leave behind?




Loadshedding was usually measured in hours without electricity, stages of power cuts or megawatts unavailable from the grid. These measures captured the immediate crisis. They tell us much less about the longer-term damage to businesses, workers and South Africa’s industrial base.




Factories do not simply return to where they were once electricity becomes reliable. During years of power shortages, firms cut jobs, postponed investment, bought expensive backup power and lost export opportunities. Some close. Others abandoned expansion plans.




The lights may thus be back on, but some of that damage remains. This matters because South Africa wants to rebuild its manufacturing sector and create more productive jobs. Ending load shedding is an essential part of that effort. But it is only the beginn

author: Saif Eddine Ghobr
title: Capacity Substitution: How Tunisia’s Problems Became Someone Else’s Priorities
content:
In the summer of 2023, a young man from Gafsa tried to cross the Mediterranean on a small boat. He did not make it. His story is one of thousands — and it is increasingly understood by Tunisian institutions through the language of border management. It is also a story about who defines what a problem is.




In June 2023, the European Commission announced a package for Tunisia: up to 

€900 million in proposed macro-financial assistance

, 

€150 million in budget support

, and 

€100 million for border management, search and rescue, anti-smuggling, and returns

. In July, the EU and Tunisia signed a 

Memorandum of Understanding

 formalising the partnership. By September, a further 

€105 million was allocated

 to migration-related programmes. By December, the €150 million budget-support programme was operational.




The sequence is documented. What it produces institutionally is less visible. This article examines a mechanism I call 

capacity substitution

. Capacity building strengthens a state’s ability to solve its own problems. Capacity substitution makes a state more efficient at solving problems defined by someone else. The distinction is simple. Its consequences are not.




Consider Tunisia’s migration apparatus. The EU–Tunisia Memorandum links European support to border management, anti-smuggling operations, search and rescue, and returns. These are legitimate E

author: Jim Loucks
title: What Washington Agreed to Last Month
content:
Berbera sits on the Gulf of Aden, about 150 miles south of Yemen. Its deep-water berth and the Emirati investment behind it are what Somaliland has been offering Washington. Illustration generated by the author, not a photograph of the port.




Somaliland’s president spent two weeks in Washington this month offering almost everything he has. Access to the port at Berbera. Access to the territory’s minerals. Military access, which he called a matter for negotiation and declined to rule out. He only asked for one thing in return. Recognition. He went home without it. The same month, the United States secured expanded security rights in Greenland and agreed in writing that sovereignty stays with Denmark.




What Somaliland Offered




Abdirahman Mohamed Abdullahi, known as Irro, arrived on September 5 for his first visit to the United States since winning Somaliland’s presidency in November 2024. On the 14th, he gave the keynote address at the Hudson Institute, at an event titled 

Somaliland as a Strategic Partner in the Horn of Africa

.




His pitch was the seaport. Irro described Berbera as a modern deep water facility that United States Africa Command had already assessed and in which the Emirati operator DP World has 

invested $442 million

. More than twelve percent of global maritime trade passes through the Bab el-Mandeb strait every day. He argued that Somaliland has

author: Regine Nguini
title: African Newsrooms Can No Longer Delay Creating the Conditions for Women to Stay
content:
When one Black South African journalist decided to leave the profession after only four years, she did not walk away because she had stopped believing in journalism: ‘I mourned because I knew I could have done so much in that space.’




Her experience is documented in a 

2025 Reuters Institute fellowship paper by South African journalist Bongekile Macupe

. After difficult experiences in the newsroom, including during her pregnancy, the journalist eventually decided to leave. Yet her words suggest that what disappeared with her departure was not her passion for journalism, but the possibility of what she might have contributed had the conditions allowed her to stay.




That sense of loss is part of what the 

Kigali Declaration on the Elimination of Gender Violence in and through Media in Africa by 2034

 is trying to prevent.




Led by African Women in Media (AWiM), the Declaration calls for action across the media ecosystem; from media organisations and professional associations to journalists, journalism educators, funders, digital platforms and regulators, to address gender violence both within media institutions and through the content they produce.




Its ambition builds on a problem that has been documented for years: for many women journalists across Africa, entering a newsroom is only the first step. Staying, progressing and practising journalism without discrimin

author: Charlize Tomaselli
title: Not Energy, But Power: why Geothermal Energy Benefits Everyone in Iceland but not Kenya
content:
This article draws on in-person interviews at Mt Suswa, Olkaria, and Menengai with

 

Coalition for Human Rights in Development

 (CHRD) members and partners directly affected by geothermal projects. Interviews were led by the Coalition’s Research and Learning Facilitator and interviewees identified through the

 

Community Resource Exchange

 (CRE), 

a system to facilitate collaborations and co-develop strategies with and among communities defending their rights in the context of international investments and development projects. The analysis also incorporates a review of Kenyan and Icelandic energy policy documents and insights from the Coalition’s roles in the

 

AfDB Civil Society Working Group

 and its Energy Sub-Group.




 

In Iceland, geothermal energy – one of the cleanest solutions to the climate crisis – is widely hailed as a success story. It supplies 

65 % of the country’s electricity

 and heats 

nearly 90%

 of its households. Everyone benefits from it.




Thousands of kilometres away, in Kenya, steam rising from the Rift Valley drives one of Africa’s 

largest geothermal programmes

, supplying 

nearly half of the country’s electricity

. According to recent data, Kenya is the world’s 

sixth-largest geothermal producer

. Yet, its projects are entangled in disputes over land, livelihoods and rights, with local communities left grappling with acid rai

author: Habib Badawi
title: The Salvador Pass: How a Nameless Desert Gap Became a Battleground for Libya’s Warlords
content:
A failed prisoner exchange in Niger has revealed a complex network of Libyan, Nigerien, Chadian, and Russian interests converging on one of the Sahara’s most established smuggling corridors.




On the maps that colonial cartographers drew of the Sahara, most features carry the names of the people who ‘discovered’ them, or of the places they resembled. The origin of the name given to the gap in the escarpment where Libya, Niger and Algeria meet is murkier: 

old French military survey maps

 simply labelled it ‘

Passe de Salvador

,’ and no definitive account of whom or what it honours has survived into the public record. What is well documented is what the pass has been used for ever since: 

for centuries, it has been one of the best-known smuggling corridors in the Sahara

, moving fuel, cigarettes, migrants and weapons between three states at the exact point furthest from any of their capitals.




This very obscurity is significant. In the current year, the desert region surrounding the pass, sometimes referred to as the Salvador Triangle, has emerged as an active arena for both warlords and great-power politics, with implications extending well beyond southern Libya.




For readers less familiar with the region, the essential political map is this: Libya has had two rival governments since its 2014 civil war — a UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, in the west, curr

author: Amged Shwehdy
title: Cybersecurity is the Infrastructure Africa is Forgetting to Build
content:
In 

June 2024

, a ransomware attack on South Africa’s National Health Laboratory Service rendered patient records inaccessible, disrupted diagnostics and forced hospitals to cancel surgeries. The incident was a stark reminder that when essential services become digital, attacks on their underlying systems can quickly become disruptions to everyday life. It was not simply a cybersecurity incident affecting an IT network; it affected health institutions’ ability to deliver services.




This distinction matters as Africa accelerates its digital transformation. Governments and businesses across the continent are investing in digital identity systems, mobile money, instant payment platforms, e-government services and other forms of digital infrastructure that increasingly shape how people access financial services, interact with the state and participate in the economy. Yet the capacity needed to protect these systems has not expanded at anything close to the same pace. Africa is building the infrastructure of a digital economy, but it is not building enough of the capacity required to defend it.







The scale of the challenge is becoming harder to ignore. INTERPOL’s 2026 assessment documents a threat landscape in which government institutions, financial services, healthcare systems and other critical infrastructure are increasingly exposed to cyberattacks. The problem is not

author: Sergey Eledinov
title: Who Wins from Ukraine’s Drones in Mali?
content:
On 12 September, CNN 

reported

 that around fifteen Ukrainian drone specialists are working with the Azawad Liberation Front (FLA) in northern Mali. According to two Ukrainians deployed there, the group does not fight on the front line; it trains fighters and helps run operations. A Ukrainian operator told CNN that he coordinates the rebels’ operations remotely and that Ukrainians helped take Kidal earlier this year. Tuareg rebels and al-Qaeda-linked fighters attacked the town simultaneously, and Russian forces were forced to withdraw. Last week, 

Jeune Afrique

 called the story an embarrassment for Washington, which is rebuilding ties with Bamako.




What follows is a balance sheet for seven actors in the war in Mali and in the Ukrainian episode: their interests, gains and losses.







Kyiv




Interest.

 The line Kyrylo Budanov set out while still head of military intelligence (HUR): strike Russia wherever it is present. Some analysts see the African operation as cheap and potentially rewarding, since it stretches Russian resources.




Gains.

 Tactical. Ukrainian operators reportedly help the FLA locate and attack Russian convoys, and by a Ukrainian operator’s own account Kidal was taken with their help. author: Dr William Nii Ayitey Menson
title: A Child’s Fifth Birthday Should Not Depend on a Foreign Budget
content:
A fifth birthday should be unremarkable.




For too many African families, it is not.




An estimated 

4.9 million children died before reaching the age of five in 2024

, and nearly six in ten of those deaths occurred in sub-Saharan Africa. Most were preventable with interventions we already know how to deliver. In Nigeria, the latest estimate is 

116 deaths per 1,000 live births

, roughly one child in nine.




Judith Leveillee, UNICEF’s field chief in Nigeria, recently 

told 

The Independent

 that child survival will be one of two priorities in the agency’s next country programme. “These are the most basic of the basics,” she said. She also warned that short-term funding makes the slower work of strengthening systems harder.




The OECD projects that 

health aid could fall by 29 to 46 percent between 2024 and 2026

, equivalent to $5 billion to $8 billion. Those cuts will hurt. But they also force a harder question: 

how did we allow a budget decision made thousands of miles away to have this much power over whether our own children live or die?




Aid cuts are exposing weaknesses in African health systems. They did not create all of them.




I have seen this problem as a physician, hospital administrator, researcher, and now through health financing and policy. The amount of money available matters enormously. But so does what happens after it is allocated.

author: Matthew de Waal
title: Ethiopia’s Foretold War Arrives
content:
No one can claim that a return to war in Tigray and northern Ethiopia is a surprise, but it makes it no less horrifying. In just a handful of days, and after months of spiralling tensions and sporadic fighting, the ‘grey conflict’ the federal government pursued against Tigray has escalated into ‘

‘full-blown war

,’ in the words of Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) vice president Ammanuel Assefa. The atrocities of the Tigray war are all too recent in the mind; the 

estimated deaths of 600,000 people

, massacres at Axum and Adigrat, the incessant drone strikes on schools, hospitals, and industry, the rape and sexual assault of over 

120,000 girls and women

, and the harrowing consequences of the man-made famine. To be facing a return to a broader conflict not even four short years after the Pretoria agreement was signed is catastrophic, and this time, threatens to intersect with the metastasising Sudanese civil war.




On Sunday, a diverse coalition of Ethiopia’s ethnic-based opposition movements announced a 

new alliance

, unveiled by Fano commander Zemane Kassie on Tigrai TV. Among them are the TPLF, the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), and three smaller ethno-nationalist movements from Afar and the Benishangul-Gumuz regions. Ethiopian Peoples’ Fo

author: Ismail Abukar
title: Breaking the Pretoria Architecture: How Ethiopia’s Fragmented Wars Converged into a Single Existential Threat
content:
When the Pretoria Cessation of Hostilities Agreement was signed in November 2022, international observers prematurely celebrated the end of one of this century’s most devastating conflicts. The silence of the guns in Tigray was treated as a definitive roadmap toward peace. What the international community failed to see was that the Pretoria architecture did not resolve Ethiopia’s core systemic collapse; it merely localized and delayed it.




During my two years working from the African Union Headquarters in Addis Ababa as the Somali Youth Representative to the AU (2019–2021), I watched the foundational blocks of this conflict harden up close. Even then, within the diplomatic corridors of the capital, the fragile nature of the state’s security architecture was undeniable. The structural fragmentation we feared has now reached a critical flashpoint. Forces that fought on bitterly opposing sides during the Tigray war—most notably the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and the Amhara Fano national movement—have crossed a seemingly impossible ideological chasm. Beside the Oromo Liberation Army (OLA), they have forged a sweeping, nationwide military coalition with four other regional factions: the Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF), the Afar Revolutionary Democratic Unity Front (Ugugumo), the Benishangul Peoples’ Liberation Movement, and the Gumuz Peoples’ Democratic Movem

author: Fundi Skweyiya-Gushu
title: China’s Humanoid Robots: A New Test for African Technology Sovereignty
content:
For African governments, the significance of China’s humanoid-robotics programme is not that robots may one day appear on African battlefields. It is a diagnostic case of how a dual-use technology can move from commercial deployment to military relevance faster than the institutions responsible for assessing and governing it can adapt. Africa’s stake is therefore not speculative. African states already operate within global technology and defence supply chains dominated by external suppliers, including China. Humanoid robotics adds another layer to an existing problem, regarding how to acquire advanced technologies without becoming dependent on systems that governments cannot independently evaluate, secure or govern




That matters because humanoid robotics is not simply another consumer technology. It brings together artificial intelligence, machine perception, sensors, autonomous navigation, manipulation, communications and advanced manufacturing. Those capabilities can be developed for civilian purposes and subsequently adapted to military environments. The significance for Africa lies precisely in that movement across boundaries, because the continent enters this technological transition with substantial differences in technical, industrial and institutional capacity.







When civilian technology acquires military relevance

author: James Mulei
title: Reading Okot p’Bitek through eyes taught to look away
content:
In 1931, Okot p’Bitek was born in Gulu, northern Uganda. It is perhaps fitting that a man who would spend much of his life questioning what Africans had been taught to admire was himself born at a rather interesting 

intersection of worlds.

 His father, Jebedayo Opi, was a school teacher shaped by the colonial education system. His mother, Cerina Lacwaa, was an Acholi singer, dancer and storyteller, deeply rooted in the oral traditions of her people.




In 

Song of Lawino

, first written in Acholi and later translated into English, p’Bitek gave us Lawino, a woman bewildered by a husband who had become so impressed by European ways that he could barely recognise the people from whom he came. Ocol had acquired the manners of the ‘

civilised’ man

, but somewhere along the way he appeared to have misplaced himself.







In 

African Religions in Western Scholarship

, he took aim at the tendency of Western scholarship to explain African religious thought through categories that Africans themselves had not necessarily created. He called this 

‘intellectual smuggling’

. The problem was not simply that Europeans were studying Africa. It was that African realities could be repackaged through foreign categories and then returned to Africans as knowledge about themselves.




Every now and then, there has been a persistent churn of African literature calling for the decolonisa

author: Yassir Gadid
title: Türkiye’s Security Export: Why Africa’s New Air Force Costs Less Than a Fighter Jet’s Spare Parts
content:
Drones have become a primary mechanism of warfare on many fronts around the world. Those fronts range from the war between Russia and Ukraine to the conflict between the United States and Iran. Drones are used to achieve air superiority, a reconnaissance advantage, and highly precise strategic strikes along the front lines. Those strikes range from the pinpoint targeting of individual objectives to larger-scale strikes against strategic targets and infrastructure.




What makes drones a unique tool of warfare is that their low cost and ease of manufacture make them accessible to poorer nations as part of their military arsenals and more broadly to meet their needs for the modernization and development of their military industries. Türkiye has emerged as one of the leading countries in the international landscape of drone technology. The country has a history of drone manufacturing dating back to the 1990s through the drone trial using the UAV-X1 projects at the time. The technical breakthrough happened in the 2010s. An example is the Bayraktar TB2 drone system (three drones plus a ground unit) that was widely used in the war in Ukraine and which made its maiden flight in 2014.
